extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and literary style
extracted.subtask_description: A first‑person, reflective Renaissance essay exploring character, style, and conduct; the page exemplifies norms and judgments an essayist (and a person) might use about truthfulness, style, ambition, and bodily comportment. Useful as guidance for personal/philosophical essaying and self-evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about human knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I look upon the too good opinion that man has of himself to be the nursing mother of all the most false opinions... finding so great a variety of judgments, so profound a labyrinth of difficulties...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value modesty and scepticism about alleged expertise; regard human curiosity as sometimes a scourge; do not trust grand claims of knowledge — prefer acknowledging ignorance and complexity rather than presumptuous certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must not be mediocre
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Horace and Martial: mediocrity in poets is not permitted; 'Verum / Nihil securius est malo poetae.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets (and by extension creators) must attain genuine excellence — mediocrity is offensive and should be kept out of print; Montaigne gives the anecdote of Dionysius whose public display of poor poetry provoked public outrage as an example of the social consequences of bad art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-critique and revision of one's work
rubrics_metrics.description: 'My works are so far from pleasing me, that as often as I review them, they disgust me... When I reperuse, I blush at what I have written; I ever see one passage after another... that I consider should be erased.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should subject their own writing to strict self-judgment, expect to find faults on rereading, and be willing to erase or revise passages; hold an internal ideal and use it as a corrective even if unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish and beauty of expression are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They abandon me throughout; all I write is rude; polish and beauty are wanting: I cannot set things off to any advantage; my handling adds nothing to the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manner of expression should enhance the matter; rough or unpolished handling can spoil even a good story. Strive for luster and finish in phrasing so subject matter can be presented to advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation but beware resulting roughness
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne claims to 'endeavour to avoid art and affectation' yet admits this can lead to an 'inform and irregular way of speaking' and roughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer naturalness over contrived elegance, but check that avoidance of artifice does not produce obscurity or slovenliness; balance natural voice with attention to clarity and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance brevity with clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted maxim: 'Brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio' — 'Endeavouring to be brief, I become obscure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of expression is valuable but must not sacrifice intelligibility; brevity that causes obscurity is a fault — aim for concise yet clear phrasing and choose a moderate style when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow your natural voice while learning from masters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Both in doing and speaking I simply follow my own natural way... though my inclination would rather prompt me to imitate Seneca’s way of writing, yet I do nevertheless more esteem that of Plutarch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be true to your own manner, but study exemplary writers to borrow graces and techniques; low or popular treatment can be effective if supported by skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper language and pronunciation matter socially
rubrics_metrics.description: 'My French tongue is corrupted, both in the pronunciation and otherwise... a twang of his place of birth... offensive to ears that were purely French.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to idiom and pronunciation affects reception; regionalisms may mark and disadvantage a speaker or writer in certain social contexts — consider audience expectations for language norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the unity of body and soul; bodily presence has social consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Beauty is a thing of great recommendation... The body has a great share in our being... The first distinction... was the advantage of beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical appearance and comportment influence social standing and authority; do not entirely separate moral/mental qualities from bodily presentation when considering leadership or social effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical presence influences authority (stature and bearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discusses stature, Marius' preference for tall soldiers, Turnus marching first 'taller by a head than all the rest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commanding bodily presence can generate respect and deter enemies; for roles of command and public office, consider how appearance, carriage, and stature contribute to perceived authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness; avoid dissimulation and flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A man must not always tell all, for that were folly: but what a man says should be what he thinks, otherwise ’tis knavery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value frankness and integrity in speech over calculated dissimulation; lying and habitual dissembling corrupt trust and virtue and have corrosive societal effects — speak truthfully except where prudence definitively forbids disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not purchase uncertain hope at high cost (reject risky ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spem pretio non emo' — 'I will not purchase hope with ready money.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sufficiency and security over risking what one already possesses for uncertain advancement; ambition that hazards one's settled condition is foolish except when necessity compels risk (e.g., for those without means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constancy and avoid torment of indecisive deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne prefers 'the lowest walk' — the beaten track — because 'Doubtful ills plague us worst.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive deliberation and uncertainty are themselves a source of suffering; choosing a steady, moderate course reduces anxiety and dependence on fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory supports judgment and oratory; compensate if weak
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Memory is a faculty of wonderful use... for my part I have none at all... I could not receive a commission by word of mouth without a note-book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good memory aids complex discourse and judgment; if you lack memory, use notes, learning by heart for speeches, and constrain spoken commissions to written form to preserve method and assurance.
